newsitem.title: USA: Washington COPs rated A1 by Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Washington COPs rated A1 by Moody's.

text.p: MOODY'S ASSIGNS A1 RATING TO STATE OF WASHINGTON'S CERTIFICATES OF PARTICIPATION ISSUED FOR EQUIPMENT
Washington (State of)
State
Washington
Moody's Rating
Issue Certififcates of Participation, Series
Rating A1
Sale Amount $1,190,000.00
Expected Sale Date 07/15/97
Rating Description Certificates of Participation
(Equipment)

NEW YORK, July 14, 1997 -- The A1 rating assigned to the equipment certificates is derived in part from the credit standing of the State of Washington which, through its State Finance Committee, has agreed to make lease payments for the financed equipment. In 1991, the State began a program of financing equipment purchases through lease backed issues. The current issuance is being offered under a Master Financing Contract, dated April 1, 1997, between the State Finance Committee and the Washington Finance Officers Association (WFOA), a Washington nonprofit corporation. Certificate proceeds are used to finance a variety of equipment purchases which have been deemed essential by each leasing agency, as well as by the State Treasurer's Office. The financing term for each equipment purchase correlates with its expected useful life, generally at least three years. On July 15, the state plans to sell approximately $1.19 million in certificates of participation (Series 1997D), proceeds of which will be used by state agencies for a variety of equipment purchases.
CERTIFICATES ISSUED UNDER MASTER FINANCING CONTRACT; LEASE PAYMENTS SUBJECT TO APPROPRIATION.

Under the terms of the Master Financing Contract, the State Treasurer will enter into an agency sublease agreement with certain state agencies for personal property. The certificates are secured by agency lease payments, which are paid from lump-sum state appropriations to each agency. The lease payments are dependent on biennial legislative appropriations to participating state agencies, and may also be subject to mid-year executive order reductions by the governor. However, the obligation to make lease payments is not subject to abatement, and will not be released, discharged or diminished for any reason including any damage or destruction to the equipment.

The risk to debt service of non-appropriation and mid-year reduction is mitigated by the nature of the lump-sum appropriations to the agencies and by the agency sublease agreements which require that agencies use all available appropriated funds for lease payments.

WFOA, as master lessor, sells, assigns and conveys to The Bank of New York, as fiscal agent, all its right, title and interest in, under and to master financing contract. Moody's expects to receive, by the closing date of the certificates, opinions from certificate counsel indicating that in the event of a bankruptcy filing by Washington State Finance Officers Association, payments to certificate holders would not be subject to disruption, delay or recovery.
The Aa1 long term on the state's general obligation bonded indebtedness reflects the following credit factors:
FUNDAMENTAL ECONOMIC RESTRUCTURING PRODUCES DIVERSIFICATION AND GROWTH

Diversification of the state's economy is evident in an economic expansion that has continued unabated since the early 1980s despite significant variation in the performance of The Boeing Company's aerospace operations. In earlier decades, Boeing determined the state's economic fortunes, and at its peak in 1969 accounted for 10% of state employment. Now, with 87,000 Washington employees, Boeing accounts for only 3% of the state job base. Growth in the state's service sector employment has offset a decline in overall manufacturing employment since 1981, and Washington's employment distribution for both sectors now more closely mirrors that of the nation. Even so, the state's economy has outperformed the nation's consistently throughout the 1990s.
SOUND FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE EXPECTED TO CONTINUE

Washington has posted a consistent trend of positive financial operating results since its recovery from the recession of the early 1980s, even during the relatively mild early 1990s recession, and this financial performance is expected to continue. Recently updated forecasts indicate larger than expected revenues for FY 1997 due to strong economic performance. As a result, the undesignated General Fund balance for fiscal 1997 is now estimated at approximately $478 million, up from $414 million forecast earlier in the year.
RECENTLY ENACTED BUDGET INDICATES STRUCTURAL BALANCE

To date, the state has accommodated the parameters of Initiative 601 passed by voters in 1993 without strain, reflecting a healthy underlying balance between service demands and revenue capacity. Although earlier projections indicated that demographic factors such as the relatively more rapid rate of growth of such populations as school children or state prisoners might make Initiative 601 difficult to absorb for the 1997-99 period, these pressures have proved manageable. Looking ahead, higher education and corrections are likely to present the greatest spending pressure beginning in the year 2000.

The Legislature passed a 1997-99 General Fund budget of approximately $19 billion, which meets the 601 spending limit with a small margin and projects an unreserved fund balance of $595 million at the end of the next biennium. Policy differences between the Governor and the Legislature were modest.
ABOVE-AVERAGE DEBT LEVELS REFLECT GROWTH-RELATED FINANCINGS

Strong population growth continues, with growth more than double the national rate between 1990 and 1996. The resulting infrastructure needs have led to growth in bonded indebtedness, and debt ratios that exceed comparable medians by a wide margin. Although the debt load is high, it is closely controlled as a budget burden. Debt service requirements as a percentage of expenditures have remained steady, and actually dropped in FY 1996.
